title: 《小小梦魇3》「海岸」DLC发售宣传视频
text: 重逢后，小洛与小寂一同穿越镜子。少了小角，他们再次只剩彼此。肮脏石头、鱼腥味与潮湿海风，无疑都代表他们来到了「海岸」。四面八方笼罩的浓雾不时被灯塔的光束划破。只要登上那里，他们就能找到方向。小洛的地图是这么说的。那就肯定没错。灯塔近在眼前，若想抵达，就必须冒险。小洛与小寂不得不潜入下水道，而水流至今仍在敞开的管线奔涌着。破裂阀门、锋利螺旋桨与淹水房间挡在前方，迫使他们必须善用每一口气，并使出全身上下所有力气。《小小梦魇3》「海岸」DLC现已推出。

title: 《007 初露锋芒》本周将推出免费DLC
text:
新任务或将登场
《007 初露锋芒》本周晚些时候将推出新的免费DLC。
IO Interactive在社交媒体上发布短视频预告，确认这款免费DLC将于10月1日推出，但目前仍未透露具体内容。不过，根据视频中疾驰而过的那辆汽车来看，我们或许可以推测，它就是玩家期待已久的阿斯顿·马丁Valhalla更新。游戏自发售以来就在主菜单中预告过这部分内容，如今看来，它终于要加入游戏了。这辆车曾在游戏接近尾声的一场大型演出场面中登场。玩家已经等了这么久，很难想象更新只会包含一项简短的战术模拟任务。它也可能加入此前在游戏整体更新路线图中公布的其他内容，例如新游戏＋、新装备，以及其他任务和内容。
不过，具体会有哪些内容，我们还得耐心等待。《007 初露锋芒》还计划推出一款以海盗之王、军阀巴瓦马为主角的剧情DLC，这个角色由Lenny Kravitz饰演。该DLC尚无确切发售日期，而且预计会是付费追加内容，不会像本周晚些时候推出的更新那样免费。
《007 初露锋芒》的Switch 2版本也仍在开发中。这个版本原本预计此时已经推出，但最近延期到了2027年，以确保玩家能获得尽可能好的体验。IO Interactive打算为本作提供多久的后续支持，目前尚不清楚；《杀手》发售多年后仍不断获得更新。即便没有持续不断的发售后内容，《007 初露锋芒》也已经大获成功：游戏在上市前三个月卖出了400万份，续作预计也会推出，不过恐怕还要等上一段时间。

title: 吉田修平：索尼和任天堂应尽量延续本世代主机
text:
下一代还不急
面对不断飙升的成本，以及已经导致PS5和Switch 2涨价的现实，索尼和任天堂需要尽可能延长现有主机的生命周期。前PlayStation全球工作室负责人吉田修平向The Verge表示，主机厂商应专注于让当前硬件平台「尽可能长时间」地持续运营。
目前没有迹象表明任天堂计划在近期推出Switch 3，毕竟Switch 2去年才上市！不过，任天堂一直会将部分预算用于研究未来硬件。今后，该公司无疑也会考虑升级首发版Switch 2，就像推出Switch Lite和Switch OLED一样。
至于索尼，我们知道PS6终将在某个时间到来。此前，分析师曾认为该主机可能于2028年推出，但索尼尚未正式透露PS6的发售时间。随着时间推移，2028年末发售的可能性似乎越来越低。吉田修平还表示，主机厂商如今或许正考虑尽可能推迟下一代硬件的到来。
吉田修平表示：「索尼和任天堂已经卖出了足够多的本世代硬件，因此考虑到商品成本，两家公司可能会考虑推迟下一代主机的发售。我认为，他们应该尽可能延长本世代的生命周期，因为玩家对使用PS5和Switch 2感到非常满意。」他继续说道：「人们的预算是有限的，而PC和主机这些设备所专用的零部件，价格涨幅似乎远高于其他娱乐形式。拥有PS5、Switch 2或PC的人，可能会继续满意地用它们玩游戏，不一定会考虑更换设备。」
这里的关键问题在于计算机内存成本暴涨，而人工智能数据中心的兴起是推高成本的部分原因。简而言之，内存生产资源有限，明年的大部分产能已经被预订。以索尼为例，如果该公司想在近期开始生产新主机，可能根本无法达到理想的产量，更不用说以消费者愿意接受的价格出售了。
作为参考，索尼推出PS5时，带光驱版本售价为500美元，纯数字版售价为400美元。如今，这两款主机的售价分别为650美元和600美元，自2020年以来分别上涨了150美元和200美元。与此同时，PS5 Pro上市时售价为700美元，如今已涨至900美元。很难想象PS6的售价会大幅低于1000美元。Switch 2的价格则从去年发售时的450美元上涨至500美元，涨幅为50美元。
此外，消费者和开发者普遍没有表现出对性能大幅提升主机的强烈需求，吉田修平也提到了这一点。唯一的例外是XBOX，该品牌一直更积极地宣传通过Project Helix迈向下一代产品。不过，微软团队与索尼、任天堂的不同之处在于，近来并没有卖出大量主机。
吉田修平总结道：「我不认为有很多玩家在要求更强的性能，开发者也没有这样的要求。我不认为开发者在要求更好的硬件！所以我认为，索尼和任天堂的本世代主机未来许多年仍会表现得相当不错。XBOX团队希望改变竞争格局，因此他们会面临困难，但现在轮到他们登场了。接下来一年会发生什么，令人非常期待。」

title: 《巫师3：狂猎-重制版》保留低模鸽子
text:
咕咕咕
《巫师3：狂猎-重制版》加入了大量画面改进，但开发商CDPR保留了一种极其重要的生物原样不动：鸽子。
在重制版公开发售前，玩家曾在游戏中发现更新后的鸽子模型，但这似乎只适用于停在地面上的鸽子。尽管如此，还是有人因以为鸽子模型发生变化而感到失望。一名用户在Reddit上发布了新的地面鸽子模型和旧的飞行鸽子模型，并配文道：「虽已离去，却永远不会被遗忘。」
幸运的是，这只备受喜爱的低多边形鸽子似乎在重制版中幸存了下来。Kotaku主编Ethan Gach在X上偶然发现了它。显然，《巫师3》会为飞行中的鸽子和停在地面上的鸽子使用不同模型！在更新后的光照效果下，低多边形鸽子反而显得更加滑稽，也更能凸显它细节的缺乏。
所以，尽管《巫师3：狂猎-重制版》带来了大量画面改进，但一些旧素材似乎仍保留在游戏中。希望CDPR也保留了游戏里那些低细节食物。《巫师3：狂猎-重制版》发售才几个小时，就已经打破了玩家人数纪录。它已经超过这款11年前游戏在Steam上的最高同时在线人数，而且随着周末临近，这一数字看起来还会继续上升。

title: 《GTA6》今年或无缘年度游戏提名
text:
赶不上投票了？
《GTA6》今年甚至可能没有资格角逐TGA的年度游戏奖。
演员、游戏编剧及前游戏记者Alanah Pearce在最近的一场直播中表示，她认为《GTA6》今年很难横扫TGA，原因在于游戏的发售时间。Pearce指出，历史上符合TGA提名资格的游戏，其资格截止日期通常都在今年《GTA6》发售日的前后。尽管有人反驳称，去年的截止日期是11月21日，比《GTA6》今年的发售日晚两天，但这仍然引发了一些合理的疑问。
最重要的问题是：评委们真的能在提名投票前通关《GTA6》吗？如果不能，他们又是否愿意在没有通关的情况下为游戏投票？这无疑会给投票流程带来许多伦理层面的疑虑。不过，也有一些办法可以提高Rockstar的机会。首先，TGA负责人Geoff Keighley可以直接推迟投票截止日期。这并非完全不可能，毕竟Keighley确实喜欢办一场精彩的节目，而《GTA6》横扫奖项也会为活动带来大量关注。
另一种可能是，Rockstar可以在截止日期前让评委提前很长时间体验游戏。目前很难判断Rockstar针对评测者制定了什么计划，但这种策略无疑会让游戏更容易获得提名。不过，这其中仍然存在太多变数。我们目前只能进行推测，但如果《GTA6》因某种原因无法参加今年的评选，它可以在2027年再试一次，而且仍有机会。外界盛传Rockstar将在明年推出《GTA6》的线上模式，这无疑会为游戏带来强劲的第二波势头。如果这足以让它与其他重量级作品竞争，Rockstar或许就能参加2027年的奖项角逐。

title: 前《战神》创作者澄清针对《劳菲》的争议言论
text:
停止骚扰
初代《战神》游戏的创作者、联合编剧兼导演David Jaffe，已经澄清了自己针对《战神：劳菲》创意总监Ariel Lawrence的争议言论。
Ariel Lawrence从第一款《战神》开始就参与了这一系列。不过，创作者David Jaffe在2007年离开该系列并创办自己的工作室后表示，自己在圣莫妮卡工作室任职期间始终和她相处不来。2026年9月，Jaffe在直播中观看《战神：劳菲》相关影像时，谈到了两人充满矛盾的工作关系。他声称，两人的性格存在冲突，而且他感觉Lawrence并没有真正热爱他们正在制作的游戏。
他一开始说道：「我完全不反对女性导演。这位女士在我们制作第一款《战神》时，还是一名助理制片人。她和我始终相处不来。她觉得我有点讨厌，而我觉得她很自命不凡。她没有把观众放在首位。在《战神》项目中，和我相处不来的人，在我看来更在意『我想在企业世界里混得好……我想玩这场游戏』，而不是『我带着一个愿景来到这里，我会为了这个愿景和你拼到底』。我觉得她缺少激情，而且在我看来，她也是个喜欢评判别人的混蛋。」
Jaffe还抨击了Cory Barlog制作《战神：劳菲》这件事本身，称这是一款「愚蠢」的游戏，并质问为什么不能「把Ariel叫到面前说，『这还没准备好』」。Jaffe的言论不出意料地走红，在《战神》粉丝群体以及更广泛的游戏社区中引发了争论。不久后，Jaffe在X上进一步解释了自己的言论，并批评那些利用他的话在网上骚扰Lawrence的人。
他写道：「听着，我个人不喜欢Ariel，而且我不认为我们共事时她有多喜欢我。我们就像油和水，属于截然不同的两类人。老实说，她在团队里可能比我更受欢迎。你看，如果你还没注意到的话，我这个人可能正如我的前妻所说，『很难搞』。所以，在这段视频中，我只是在回应并分享我们共事经历中的这一面。无论过去的经历是好是坏，这都是我谈论前同事时唯一会采用的方式。有人拿我和Ariel的经历当借口或跳板，对她发起人身攻击，这种做法既卑劣又糟糕。她是一个真实的人，和你一样，有自己的生活和感受，也有在乎她、爱她的人。这样做真的残酷得要命。」
遗憾的是，《战神：劳菲》一直是网络上的攻击目标，而Jaffe的言论又给这场风波添了一把火。6月首次公布该作由女性担任主创时，网络恶意骚扰者对Deborah Ann Woll外貌的评论，以及他们对于女性主导《战神》游戏的愤怒，彻底席卷了社交媒体上的游戏圈。这种相互指责似乎并未停止，只是放慢了速度。此后，其他游戏也承受了互联网情绪带来的冲击，Insomniac的《漫威金刚狼》引发的争论就是例子。不过，《战神：劳菲》仍然因此遭受了无端攻击。《最后生还者》导演Bruce Straley还以该作为例，说明现代3A游戏为何不再让他感到「兴奋」——尽管他后来为这番言论道了歉。
《战神：劳菲》将于2027年2月16日发售，独占登陆PS5。

title: 《暗黑破坏神4》总监：续作发售后仍会支持本作
text:
列车不会停下
《暗黑破坏神5》公布后，粉丝开始担心《暗黑破坏神4》还能运营多久。《暗黑破坏神4》总监Brent Gibson表示，大家不必担心。
《暗黑破坏神5》在2026年暴雪嘉年华亮相，让粉丝既兴奋又担忧。玩家当然期待《暗黑破坏神》新作，但《暗黑破坏神4》才于2023年推出，这么快就公布续作，让仍在玩前作的玩家觉得它似乎快要走到尽头了。
不过，《暗黑破坏神4》总监Brent Gibson表示，无须为此担心。他接受Icy Veins采访时谈到了游戏未来的内容计划，并表示即使《暗黑破坏神5》发售，团队仍会继续支持《暗黑破坏神4》。
他先打了个比方：「如果你站在时代广场中央，举着末日将至的牌子，那末日其实并没有来。我们还有很多内容要推出，亚马逊职业也会在之后加入。这列车不会停下。我喜欢这个世界的一点是，我们做的不只是一个游戏系列，而是一个完整的宇宙。我们甚至还在为《暗黑破坏神2》加入术士职业。很少有游戏系列能像我们这样，让玩家持续玩下去；我们也了解自己的玩家群体。如果你担心，那就放宽心，因为我们还会在很长一段时间里继续制作内容。不过，我们也对《暗黑破坏神5》感到兴奋。我们还有一部剧集要推出。不必再等上十年才能看到更多内容了。现在的情况很令人振奋。」
具体来说，Gibson表示，只要玩家还愿意参与，暴雪就计划继续为《暗黑破坏神4》推出赛季内容。他还特别提到，暴雪至今仍在支持《暗黑破坏神2》和《暗黑破坏神3》。他表示：「现在仍有人在玩那些游戏。只要你们还来玩，我们就会继续制作内容。」正如Gibson所说，《暗黑破坏神4》将在2027年上半年加入亚马逊职业。距离《暗黑破坏神5》发售还有三年，开发团队仍有充足时间为前作加入更多职业和玩法。今年的暴雪嘉年华上，他们也在《暗黑破坏神》专题座谈中谈到了这件事。
《暗黑破坏神5》总监Joe Shely表示：「《暗黑破坏神4》的后续支持前景很好，团队会全力支持这款游戏。就在今天早些时候，我们宣布亚马逊职业和地狱遗赠赛季将加入《暗黑破坏神4》，游戏也将登陆Switch 2。我们还会继续支持《暗黑破坏神4》，玩家有很多理由继续玩下去。」
制作总监Tiffany Wat补充道：「每款游戏都有专门的团队负责，因为它们对我们和玩家社群都非常重要。我认为，这让我们有很好的机会相互交流、共同协作。虽然我们分属不同团队，但合作依然十分紧密，因为说到底，我们都是在为《暗黑破坏神》的玩家制作游戏。我觉得现在是成为《暗黑破坏神》粉丝的最好时候。」

title: 2026 indiePlay中国独立游戏大赛入围名单公布！
text:
今年 indiePlay 中国独立游戏大赛迎来了第 12 届！从 2015 年起，indiePlay 见证与陪伴了中国独立游戏的成长，活动在挖掘和鼓励游戏作品的同时也成为连结国内外游戏开发者的桥梁。如今 indiePlay 已经成长为在全球具有一定知名度的活动，2026 年 indiePlay 中国独立游戏大赛共收到来自全球超 30 个国家和地区的超 700 款游戏报名。
indiePlay 通过各项奖项鼓励开发者游戏玩法、叙事、设计上的不断追求以及视觉、听觉等艺术表达上的不断探索。同时，活动也始终聚焦行业创新，本届赛事全新增设 AI 游戏专属赛道，旨在引导开发者跳出素材生成式的浅层应用，深度探索 AI 技术与游戏核心玩法、交互设计、关卡逻辑、叙事体验等核心内容的深层应用。
今年报名作品数量与整体质量的提升，给到了大赛评委们全新的挑战。入围名单的评选比往年更加纠结，因此最终公布的时间也延后了一周。在经过 2 个月线上以及线下的多轮反复评审商议之后，最终得出了 2026
indiePlay 中国独立游戏大赛的入围名单。在此感谢所有评委们对于活动的辛勤付出！

title: NOVA海外独立游戏见闻 Vol.154
text:
Vol.154（9 月第 4 周）
本期见闻覆盖时间：9 月 21 日至 9 月 27 日
本期整理： CoryluS
行业见闻录
2026 Green Games Jam 圆满落幕，颁发 11 项奖项
9 月 21 日， 媒体 GamesIndustry.biz 报道 ，此前于英国伦敦的 BFI Southbank 举行的绿色游戏创作活动成果评选 Green Games Jam Awards 2026（GGJA）圆满结束，对 2026 年 Green Game Jam（GGJ）的优秀作品进行了表彰，共颁发 9 个游戏奖项和 2 项特别荣誉：
《Seekers Notes》——最佳新人
《Orna: The GPS RPG》——最佳小型工作室、UNEP 之选
《Hope’s Adventure》——最佳珊瑚礁作品
《Lords Mobile》——最佳雨林作品
《Flutter: Butterfly Sanctuary》——最佳叙事
《Angry Birds Friends》与《Angry Birds Dream Blast》——最佳筹款
《Splash – Fish Aquarium》——Google 之选
《Hay Day》——玩家之选
Maria Sayans（来自 ustwo games）——个人荣誉奖项“Champion”
CD Projekt Red——Changemaker（因其华沙工作室推动环保化相关工作）
本届 GGJA 由 Playing for the Planet 主办，旨在表彰电子游戏行业在可持续游戏开发以及环境主题内容创作方面取得的成果。Playing for the Planet 运营负责人 Lisa Pak 表示：“每年，GGJ 都会展示游戏如何将环境故事带入现实，并激励玩家保护和恢复我们的星球”。她期待在 2027 年第八届 GGJ 中，继续与全球数百万玩家围绕“韧性”这一主题展开讨论。
图片：gamesindustry.biz
同一发行商单日发布 29 款抢先体验游戏
9 月 21 日， 媒体 PC Gamer 报道称 ，独立发行商 Hard Shark Games 于 9 月 15 日在 Steam 一次性发布 29 款游戏，全部为抢先体验作品，题材涵盖竞速、零售模拟、生存恐怖、体育、飞行模拟和 2D 平台等类型。29 款游戏均由 Hard Shark Games 同时担任开发商，且多款作品的抢先体验说明使用了高度相似的固定文案。
Hard Shark Games 的行为也引起了玩家对其作品制作方式和发行目的的讨论，批评其高频率、批量化的发行方式，该发行商旗下游戏的 Steam 商店页面用户评价中也有不少玩家表达了对这些游戏质量的不满。而此前，Steam 鉴赏家 Sentinels of the Store 就曾在 2025 年 3 月 4 日发帖 整理了 Hard Shark Games 当时发行的大量作品，并提出了关于批量发布、使用 Unity 现成素材、涉嫌直接复用或盗用其他游戏内容等方面的质疑。
Hard Shark Games 近日发行的游戏《Supermarket Life Simulator》/图片： Steam 商店
MobyGames 推出专业版以完善开发者履历
9 月 24 日， 媒体 GamesIndustry.biz 报道称 ，游戏数据库 MobyGames 正在通过名为“MobyGames Professional”的付费服务进一步面向游戏从业者提供职业相关功能。MobyGames 长期保存游戏及其开发者信息，但开发者过去只能通过网站已有资料展示自己的游戏履历。此次加入认领功能后，用户可以将自己的账户与对应的公开开发者页面关联，并在经过验证后补充个人资料。该服务于今年 6 月进入测试阶段，1.0 正式版本计划于今年秋季推出，月费为 14.99 美元，按年订阅折合每月 11.99 美元，并提供 45 天免费试用。
MobyGames 产品经理 Reece Denzel 表示，认领功能不会允许开发者自行修改游戏履历中的结构性信息——例如改变某款游戏的正式署名名单。开发者能够修改的是个人信息以及与自身经历有关的补充内容，这些内容会被标记为来自经过验证的开发者本人。另外，MobyGames Professional 还加入了个人作品集功能：开发者可以围绕自己的游戏履历建立作品集页面，上传或关联演示视频、截图以及其他作品链接，并针对具体项目进一步说明自己承担的工作。除此之外，MobyGames 计划进一步利用数据库中的游戏、人员和公司信息提供行业分析，包括招聘市场、薪资范围、不同地区的就业情况以及企业招聘和裁员等数据。
图片： gamesindustry.biz
任天堂获判 450 万美元 Switch 盗版赔偿
9 月 26 日， 媒体 Eurogamer 报道称 ，美国华盛顿州西区联邦地区法院已于 9 月 23 日对 James Williams 作出默认判决（default judgment），要求这名曾担任 Reddit 社区 r/SwitchPirates 版主、网络昵称为“Archbox”的用户向任天堂赔偿 450 万美元（约 340 万英镑）。根据法院签署的裁定，法院支持了任天堂此前要求按照每款游戏（共 30 款）赔偿 15 万美元的赔偿诉求，并认定在相关行为具有故意侵权性质的情况下，该赔偿额度适当。同时，法院发布永久禁令，禁止 Williams 继续提供任何未经授权的任天堂游戏、帮助传播相关内容，或传播用于绕过任天堂游戏及主机技术保护措施的软件。法院还要求其关闭与相关侵权活动有关的网络商店及社交媒体账号。
本次案件由任天堂于 2024 年 6 月起诉，指控 Williams 经营多个提供未经授权的任天堂 Switch 游戏的网站，并通过 r/SwitchPirates 推广这些网站，同时帮助用户安装用于绕过任天堂游戏及主机技术保护措施的软件。不过，致力于报道有关盗版和数字权利信息的 博客 TorrentFreak 指出，在这起案件中，由于被告没有按照法院要求参加诉讼或进行答辩，因此法院在缺少正常双方抗辩的情况下，根据原告提交的材料，对被告作出判决。在满足特定条件的情况下，被告可以申请撤销默认判决。与此同时，Williams 此前使用的“archbox”Reddit 账号已经自行删除，任天堂起诉中提及的网站也早已关闭。
图片： eurogamer
研究：3A 高成本危机下的独立开发空间
近日，电子游戏杂志 《Edge》 发布第 428 期专题，其中的文章 “游戏行业已经破碎——我们能修复它吗？” （The game industry is broken – can we fix it?）谈及了近年来游戏行业裁员危机，并讨论了 3A 高成本危机下的独立开发空间。
文章首先讨论了游戏行业如何应对开发成本持续上升、项目规模扩大以及大量工作室关闭的问题。前 Tencent Games 业务发展总监、首届 The Game Awards “Game Changer”奖获得者 Amir Satvat 根据他所追踪的数据表示，2022 至 2026 年的累计失业人数将超过 5.8 万人，预计 2026 年将有超过 1.45 万名从业者失业，而构成当前行业危机的重要内部因素之一，是持续上涨的 3A 游戏开发成本。随后，文章提出了“制作更小型游戏”的方向。PlayStation 前高管 Shawn Layden 认为，开发商可以重新关注规模更小、更加紧凑的游戏，并鼓励开发商制作能够将整体游玩时长控制在 20 小时以内的作品。Satvat 则表示，他已经看到越来越多开发团队尝试“重新调整规模”——例如 Wildflower Interactive：该团队目前正在制作《Coven Of The Chicken Foot》，核心团队只有 11 人，音频通过联合开发完成，绑定和建模工作则进行外包。
文章同时将这一变化延伸到了独立开发商和中型发行商的生存模式。文章采访了独立开发商兼发行商 Kitfox Games 联合创始人 Tanya X Short，她谈到了风险投资近年来从科技行业向游戏行业的流入，以及投资者按照科技企业的增长逻辑看待游戏公司后，又在意识到游戏同时属于艺术和娱乐产业时迅速撤出资金的现象。文章还提到，Layden 将中型发行商的出现视为行业新的希望，并以 Kepler 推出《光与影：33 号远征队》以及 Lyrical Games 为例，认为只要维持精简的组织结构和较低的运营成本，就可以支持那些获得商业成功概率较低、但开发成本也较低的游戏。
图片： edge-online.com
开发商 Undead Labs 从 Xbox 分离为独立工作室
9 月 23 日， 据媒体 GamesIndustry.biz 报道 ，《腐烂国度》系列开发商 Undead Labs 已经完成与 Xbox 的分离，目前以“员工持有”的独立工作室形式运营。此次变化发生在微软持续推进 Xbox 业务调整之际，Undead Labs 同时确认，一批员工将面临裁员。Undead Labs 工作室负责人 Philip Holt 表示：“独立能够让我们更接近社区，也让我们能够专注于最重要的事情：尽我们所能制作最好的游戏，并赢得那些选择把时间花在我们身上的人的持续支持”。Holt 称工作室未来计划的更多细节将在后续公布。
与此同时，《腐烂国度 3》的开发仍在继续，目前已经进入 Alpha 阶段，团队正在推进此前公布的计划，目标是在今年年底前进入封闭测试，并继续以 2027 年为发售目标，登陆 XBOX、Game Pass、PC 和 PlayStation。玩家可以通过 StateofDecay.com 获取后续消息，也可以报名参加未来的《腐烂国度 3》测试。
图片： gamesindustry.biz
独游公告板
一周拾遗 ：本周值得关注的新发售、重新上架或公布新版本的独立游戏。
1. 9 月 21 日，经典 Flash 游戏《快乐轮子》（Happy Wheels）登陆 Steam。本作是一款基于物理效果的横向卷轴沙盒游戏，早年间在网页平台流行。玩家可以选择不同角色及对应载具，在障碍赛道中前进。开发者 Jim Bonacci 在游戏上线前发现，该作在 Steam 商店页面已经积累了约 75 万份愿望单。他表示，自己作为一名已经使用 Steam 超过 20 年的玩家，同时也是一名“在业内没有任何人脉”的游戏开发者，很难预料会获得如此规模的关注。截至 27 日，《快乐轮子》Steam 商店页面已收获 2796 条评测，好评率 94%。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/4705510/Happy_Wheels/
2. 9 月 24 日，独立开发团队 BLAIKE GAMES 推出动作冒险与策略生存游戏《光陨之地》（Land of Glarefall）。玩家将作为王国调查团成员，在大地图中自由探索、搜集资源并推进剧情，逐渐揭开“黑金”与魔物背后的真相。游戏采用昼夜循环，白天可以进行探索、采集、建设和剧情推进，夜晚则需要面对不断袭来的魔物。玩家可以利用木材、矿石等资源建造防御设施、恢复道具并升级装备，同时通过英雄技能树和雇佣兵系统强化战斗能力。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/3836120/_/
3. 9 月 24 日，独立开发团队 Xpercent Games 推出餐厅经营与烹饪游戏《动物厨房 Tasty Chef》。玩家既是餐厅老板，也是亲自参与厨房工作的厨师，需要自行设计工作区域、采购和储存食材、按照不同步骤制作餐点，并及时完成顾客订单。随着经营规模扩大，玩家可以自由摆放烹饪设备、储存设施和工作台，调整厨房动线，还能聘请 NPC 员工负责接单、备料、烹饪、送餐、补货等工作。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/5019920/_Tasty_Chef/
4. 9 月 25 日，《异星工厂》（Factorio）开发商 Wube Software 在官方 “Friday Facts”第 447 期 中公布了一项新的社区内容：官方现已公开《异星工厂》系列 3D 打印模型，玩家可以下载模型文件并自行打印。这项计划最初源于 2024 年《异星工厂：太空时代》开发后期的一场试玩活动：当时开发团队邀请 3D 打印机供应商 Prusa Research 参与活动，并现场尝试打印游戏中的模型，活动结束后，开发团队决定把这一计划扩展为可以面向玩家公开下载的完整模型项目。本次所公布的模型主要围绕《异星工厂》中的工厂建设元素展开，共包含 65 个独立模型，并以 247 个 STL 文件形式发布，包括传送带、机械臂、箱子、角色、石炉、电力采矿机和异虫相关单位等。Wube Software 也欢迎玩家能够在官方模型基础上继续进行修改，加入自己的设计。
https://factorio.com/blog/post/fff-447
开发追踪： 本周更新开发关键节点、尚处在开发早期或中期的独立游戏。
1. 【开发者投递】波兰独立游戏开发者Łukasz Twardowski 近期在 Steam 发布第一人称潜行游戏《PROCEDURE ZERO》的免费试玩版。主角不携带武器，也从不杀人。用香烟换情报，与狱警斗智，一区接一区拿下整座监狱。游戏支持简体中文，并带有完整中文配音，正式版将于 11 月 12 日发售。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/5147680/PROCEDURE_ZERO/
2. 近日，独立开发团队 Arcane Ermine 宣布玩具车冒险游戏《Obstacle Overdrive》将于 10 月 2 日发售，并公布 新预告片 。玩家需要在一间充满 90 年代玩具的卧室里驾驶微型遥控车，穿过由日常物品构成的各种障碍赛道，在翻越坡道、跷跷板、木桥和其他障碍的过程中完成挑战。本作提供 5 辆操控特点不同的车辆，玩家可以在游玩过程中解锁并尝试不同车型，同时收集可以戴在车辆上的帽子。
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dr5zebXpO-M
3. 9 月 21 日，合作游戏《Fish & Ships》在 PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct 2026 上发布首支预告片。玩家需要扮演鱼，共同操控飞艇，在寻找海洋的过程中穿越各种环境。不同成员分别负责驾驶、处理绳索以及维修飞船等工作，团队之间的配合将直接影响飞行过程。玩家还可以使用霰弹枪攻击其他角色，并将箱子扔出飞艇制造混乱，乐趣满满。游戏目前尚未公布发售日期。
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yvm2fDQCm2w
4. 9 月 21 日，Qloud Games 在 PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct 2026 上宣布，经过 4 年开发的生活模拟 MMO《Loftia》将于 11 月 3 日登陆 Steam 抢先体验。玩家将进入由漂浮岛屿组成的世界，每名玩家都可以拥有自己的空中岛屿，通过种植、制作、探索和装饰逐步建立自己的生活空间，并与其他玩家共同建设社区。预告片还展示了角色、宠物与房屋相关的自定义玩法内容。
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8aWeb-Q4o14
Demo 体验： 本周上线 Demo、或可一试的独立游戏一览。
1.《The Heir: Steampunk Escape Room》
关键字：探索、第一人称、悬疑；1895 年。你将扮演沃斯博士的科学继承人候选者，探索一座沉浸式维多利亚风格实验室，破解融入环境与剧情之中的精巧谜题，揭开沃斯实验背后的黑暗秘密。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/4959760
2.《Impious》
关键字：刷宝、迷宫探索、回合制战斗；你因罪孽被带到这里。收集装备，做出决策，构建角色，寻找出路。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/3119710
3.《Blu's Time Machine》
关键字：平台游戏、2D、冒险；扑腾跳跃、推进助飞、投掷扳手来击败敌人，力挽狂澜！
https://store.steampowered.com/app/5078150
4.《Squarelings》
关键字：社交聚会、平台游戏、休闲；每个关卡都是对沟通、团队协作与友谊的全新考验。支持 4–12 名玩家。
https://store.steampowered.com/app/4958920
5.《Disciple》
关键字：Roguelite、逆弹幕射击、洛夫克拉夫特式；将圆盘掷入深渊，在成群宇宙恐怖之间弹射穿梭，借助远古神器打造强力流派。

title: An ode to the loveable, horrible, wonderful Counter-Strike community and my first tournament experience
text:
"It sounds like you need to find some sense of belonging, a group you can call your own and feel at home with."
Those words, or words to that effect, are ones my therapist recently spoke to me. I think she probably had in mind something a little more traditional—church, or one of those manly men groups, something like that—but last week I found a glimpse of a solution amidst an industrial estate in Warsaw, Poland.
There, Logitech G Play 2026 was being held, including a Counter-Strike 2 tournament with a $100,000 prize pool. As I sat on a bleacher seat surrounded by Poles, despite not understanding a lick of what was being said around me or by the Polish commentators over the speakers, I felt at home.
The stage housed both teams—the Canadian team Luminosity Gaming and the French team 3DMax —facing each other, and the audience lining all four sides, with big screens above the stage on all four sides.
I had the choice to sit in the area designated for VIP and press, cordoned off and conspicuously lacking bleachers, instead housing chairs firmly planted at floor height. I chose to sit in the bleachers, though, with the hundreds of regular CS2 fans that had come to see the show. No doubt I'd heard one or two of them in my own games before, shouting expletives at me in a foreign tongue. Just how I like it. These are my people.
I've been playing Counter-Strike for well over a decade now, albeit with some breaks away from the game during that period. But apart from when CS:GO first launched, I never really got into the pro scene—I mostly preferred to just play and improve without getting too into teams and tournaments.
Sometimes that would make me feel a little disconnected from the community, when my teammates would reference games and pros that I wasn't too familiar with. I was happy enough, but being at the tournament last week made me realise what I'd been missing out on.
I suppose the feeling I experienced was the same as what sports fans get—at least, those who actually travel to see games. I'd only ever been into football of the American variety, which made in-person attendance difficult as a Brit, setting aside the occasional game at Wembley stadium.
I didn't get into it immediately. As I sat and watched, it took me a while to acclimate and get invested. It helped that I'd spoken to a couple of pro players from Luminosity the day prior, as I found the two that I spoke to—Azuwu and yxngstxr—to be very genuine and friendly people, so I felt invested in them winning (alas, they did not).
(Image credit: Future) I was grateful to be familiar with the game and the maps, because I could understand what was going on despite not understanding the commentary. But most of the first game I spent getting used to the pace and rhythm of spectator mode, having not watched a spectator CS2 game in quite a while.
Between the first and second game, plenty of people rushed away from the bleachers to go out and grab a drink or have a smoke, myself included. I didn't speak to anyone; I didn't need to. I just stood outside for a few minutes in the dwindling light, anticipating getting back on a seat and watching the next game.
There were moments in that game that felt genuinely spiritual
The second game was when I got fully invested. Which was just as well, because that game went into two overtimes, which is very rare at least in my non-pro experience. It was a long, close match, and that made it all the better.
There were moments in that game that felt genuinely spiritual, which is a crazy thing to say and you will not hear me recount again, lest my colleagues never let me live it down. The memory of seeing the AWP-er Afro clutch as the commentators ramped up the tension of their narration, and then hearing the roars all around me as he hit a ridiculous shot, is now seared into my mind.
As are the silly things, like the audience—myself included—ramping up our building roar to a crescendo as two opposing players were approaching each other without knowing. Or the between-round camera cuts to an audience member sitting on the row next to me, with his laptop out, opening loot crates, again with a building roar as he crossed his fingers for a rare skin rather than wasted money.
The few hours in their company left me very appreciative for the community and the players I've spent so much time shooting in the head over the years.
The lights, the booming and bassy audio, the whole experience has made me feel a fool for missing out on it for so long. But more than those things, it's the shared experience that I feel I've missed out on the most, the feeling of connection with others over the love of the game.
It feels silly that, for a game I've sunk so many hours into over so many years, until now I'd not tried to really connect with its loveably toxic and foul-mouthed community in-person, sharing the tournament experience.
Here's hoping for many more FaceIt matches with these people, no matter how many multi-lingual insults about my mother they throw my way. Deep down we know we love each other and this incredible game. Sometimes it just takes a bit of in-person, language-barrier'd bonding to realise it. How's that for belonging?

title: How every major character in Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment would fare if they had to survive the plot of Halo 1
text:
All other games writers are cowards. Wealth and power have conspired to intimidate them into silence, to concern themselves with trifles instead of things that actually matter. Not me, though. I'm brave, and strong; my voice won't be quieted. I don't care about the consequences that come for speaking the truth. Here is the article no other outlet dares write.
Here is how the main characters of Crime and Punishment would fare if they had to survive the plot of Halo 1.
Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov
Rodya's melee specialisation would steer him well through the Pillar of Autumn, where close quarters let him get up and close with grunts and elites, but I'm sceptical of his ability to operate autonomously in the broader, ranged theatres of Truth and Reconciliation. Assuming for the sake of argument that he was able to familiarise himself with the rhythm of focusing plasma fire to take out enemy shields before switching rapidly to the M6 pistol to finish them off, I think he would go to pieces in 343 Guilty Spark, where the horror and human tragedy of the Flood's first appearance would traumatise him to the point of paralysis.
Dmitri Prokofyich Razumikhin
Razumikhin, whose name more-or-less translates to Brain Guy, would undoubtedly prove himself a canny strategist, but his hard core of empathetic humanity would turn from asset to obstacle when it came time to butcher a room filled with sleeping grunts in Assault on the Control Room. Ultimately, Razumikhin's odds of survival would depend on whether his was a singleplayer or co-op campaign, as in the latter case he would be an adept support to a more ruthless warrior, who could make up for Dmitri's softer, academic inclinations.
Semyon Zakharovich Marmeladov
Crushed by Warthog.
Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladova
As the moral heart of Dostoevsky's novel, Sofya seems ill-suited to the demands that Bungie's seminal 2001 first-person shooter would place on her. But don't count her out; she is perhaps the book's most indefatigable character, refusing to abandon Raskolnikov to his shame and guilt over an unforgivable crime much as she might refuse to leave a platoon of marines without Scorpion tank support. Her weakness is not her combat strength but rather her intense religious faith, which could plausibly see her sign up with the Covenant as Halo 1's closest analogue to the Russian Orthodox Church.
Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikova
Raskolnikov's sister Dunya would absolutely tank the entire thing solo. Legendary difficulty, all skulls on. She's using backpack reloads and animation cancels to put ceaseless fire down range as she proceeds swiftly across classic levels like The Silent Cartographer. She knows all the level skips but doesn't use them.
Arkady Ivanovich Svidrigailov
Banned for comments on voice chat. Last online a year ago.
Pyotr Petrovich Luzhin
Dunya's doughy husband-to-be would fare poorly practically from the outset. In co-op, he would demand to drive all the vehicles but would not be skilled at it, and his insistence on hoarding rare and powerful weapons like the M41 SPNKr rocket launcher would dramatically decrease the combat effectiveness of his unit. In solo, these issues would remain, with the added drawback that he has no squad to make up for his deficiencies. One also cannot discount the possibility he would simply be so weird about Cortana he would be summarily executed by Captain Keyes.
Porfiry Petrovich
Quietly survived the events on Alpha Halo several years ago. If you search you will find him in Halo Infinite, which he's not loving.

title: Cregger's Resident Evil film is already the 3rd highest grossing RE film with over $100 million at the domestic box office in under 2 weeks
text:
Zach Cregger's take on survival horror in his recent Resident Evil film has gone down pretty well—ask just about anyone here at PC Gamer and they'll tell you how much they loved the interpretation . But it's not just done well critically, Resident Evil is also raking in the cash.
Cregger's Resident Evil earned $23 million across the US and Canada in its second week (via Fangoria ), second only to the re-release of Avengers: Endgame, which has returned to theaters in the lead up to Avengers: Doomsday. But Resident Evil did manage to beat out Brad Pitt's The Heart of the Beast and the Chris Hansen biopic Primetime, a pretty impressive achievement.
(Image credit: Sony Pictures Entertainment) $23 million may not sound like a lot, especially when you chalk it up against the whopping $75 million Sony Pictures spent making the film, so it's a good thing that Resident Evil has made way more money overall. Looking at The Numbers , Cregger's Resident Evil is already the third most lucrative movie in the Resident Evil film franchise, with $60 million earned in its opening weekend, $103 million in total domestic box office, and an impressive $197 million in the worldwide box office.
Interestingly, Cregger's Resident Evil is easily the top domestic box office Resident Evil film ever, with Paul W. S. Anderson's Resident Evil: Afterlife taking second place, and Resident Evil: Degeneration and Extinction vying for third place.
But the worldwide box office tells a different story. Here, Cregger's Resident Evil remains in fourth place, behind Resident Evil: The Final Chapter's $314 million, as well as Resident Evil: Afterlife and Resident Evil: Retribution.
The overall standings for top five grossing Resident Evil films— so far —are as follows:
Resident Evil: Afterlife - $356,002,756
Resident Evil: The Final Chapter - $340,945,882
Resident Evil - $300,364,617
Resident Evil: Retribution - $282,993,160
Resident Evil: Extinction - $200,519,782
Cregger's Resident Evil still has some ground to make up but with it only being out for a couple of weeks now I'm pretty confident in its ability to rise above the rest.

title: My GTA 5 install has a death wish but I have soothed it with flossing
text:
Los Santos Customs
I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier .
There is an anxiety to my movements now. The stench of death lingers about Grand Theft Auto 5 like petrichor after hard, hot rain, and I am nervous that any addition will finally nudge it over the edge.
As we've previously established, the game now only launches properly in windowed mode, and once it churns through all the modifications I have burdened it with, it deposits me in an empty void where Franklin Clinton's house used to be, sending him tumbling through the abyss. Every time I load GTA 5, Franklin screams.
Anyway, I added a new mod. It's called Fortnite Floss Dance [OIV] and it adds "Smooth looping Floss dance, same speed as Fortnite." Convenience is its philosophy: whenever you begin flossing, music will play automatically, so you don't look weird. Don't like the music? Its volume is controlled by a slider. Also, the entire UI is in Arabic, which I did not expect when I downloaded it but which adds something indefinable that I like a lot.
What to say? Franklin flosses now. He flosses indiscriminately, indefatigably. Nothing can deter him. The ongoing chaos of a semi-deleted Los Santos does not faze him. His endlessly perishing and replenishing bodyguards do not concern him. Smash him with a car and he will only right himself and keep going. There is only him, the music, and a command in a language I do not speak but which I must assume reads 'Begin flossing'.
(Image credit: Rockstar) Videogames are so cool.

title: Toem 2 review: A sweet sequel that's a tad too easy to be memorable
text:
Need To Know
What is it?: A quest-y adventure game where snapping a pic is always the answer.
Release date: September 29, 2026
Expect to pay: $17 / £13.59
Developer: Something We Made
Publisher: popagenda
Reviewed on: Intel Core Ultra 7 265, RTX 5070 Ti, 32GB RAM
Multiplayer: No
Steam Deck: Verified
Link: Steam
Adventure games are full of people with problems that need solvin' and in Toem 2 , just as in the original, the solution is usually a fresh photo with my slick vintage dynamic zoom camera. This time grandma is sending me to catch the bus to see the elusive blooming of the whirling birch tree. I can only get a ticket to the next town by completing quests at each stop along the way.
In each of the four towns I've got the freedom to explore, looking for locals who need whatever assistance I can provide with my surprisingly versatile multi-attachment camera. For my trouble, they'll stamp my journal, and my quest continues when I've got enough stamps to visit the next stop on the bus line.
What kinds of camera-based help do the people of Toem 2 need?
A farmer needs me to photograph the hiding spots of four runaway garden gnomes.
A gardener wants me to source some inspo pics of creative non-pots for plants.
A trio of dandelions want photographic proof that their missing sibling isn't truly lost.
Some quests are more traditional adventure game tasks sans-camera
A scaredy cat scarecrow wants me to carry him to a new perch without any pesky birds.
A knight with a serious boo-boo needs a potion to cure their injuries.
There's an escape room in the city with a prize waiting for whoever can crack it.
Toem 2 has lots of collectible outfits. The big mascot version of my character's own head is my favorite.
Like the original, I've also got a compendium of critters I can snap if I want to be a completionist.
The airborne camera tripod for advanced selfie mode is very fun to mess around with. Sometimes I'd stand on top of a table or obstacle and deploy my heli-camera out into the air to take a bird's eye shot.
It's all a little too automatic
In the original Toem, I just needed to collect enough stamps from any quest in an area to hop onto the bus to the next destination. Toem 2 has a much clearer main quest for each area. Every locale has a combo of a special camera attachment and a hapless local who needs my assistance using it before I continue my journey. Helping these folks isn't required, but is definitely the intended path to a friend-filled ending.
Each attachment has a non-camera function (the first one is a pair of scissors) that I use by aiming my viewfinder and pressing a button.
The streamlined quest structure tells a cute story.
But it loses some of the adventure game magic.
Good adventure games (the original Toem among them) produce that really electrifying puzzle solving sensation. You see a problem. You imagine a few possible solutions. You walk around and eventually… "ohhhhhh, now I see!"
You know that saying? "To a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail." Toem 2 gave me a hammer and then actually did present me only with nails. I mostly don't need to think creatively to understand a problem. I just have to walk around until I see the next obvious use of my camera ability.
In my favorite adventure games, quests are almost riddle-like hints instead of direct instructions. The joy comes from the moment my brain "clicks" with the answer I've been searching for. In Toem 2 I'm doing a whole lot of camera clicking but very little brain clicking. It's a quick and sweet sequel, but the easy-peasy objectives make it feel less innovative than the original.

title: UK government wants people to be rude to AI: 'You don't need to say thank you'
text:
The government of the United Kingdom is reminding its employees that they do not need to thank AI systems when they produce an output, even in cases where that output is correct. The helpful note is included as part of the government's guidelines on " using AI ethically and sustainably ," and arises not out of a need to remember that these things are absolutely not sentient or "alive" in any way whatsoever, but simply because, well, they're horrifically expensive and bad for the planet.
The guidelines (via Tom's Hardware ) are a draft document, and serve only as "a starting point to support your AI journey." And for the most part, it's common sense stuff: Check the outputs carefully to ensure they're accurate and unbiased, and don't provide any inputs that you don't want used for training purposes, because in all likelihood it will be.
There's also a note that you own, and are responsible for, the work: Multi-billion-dollar AI companies may be able to point the finger at " rogue agents " but career civil servants have no such escape clause.
But it's the "don't thank your AI" bit that really leaps out at me, one of three guidelines to using AI efficiently, "to reduce the environmental impact:
Keep your prompts short, clear and direct
Use as few prompts as possible ( you don’t need to say thank you )
Only use AI when needed
I used to sometimes thank the bank machine when it spat out my cash, a habit I would silently justify to myself with the thought that good manners are good to encourage. These days, though, I'm more of a Ron Swanson about the whole thing:
(Image credit: NBC) Frankly, I think 'recognizing the psychological dangers of anthropomorphizing LLMs' is probably the best reason for being rude to machines. But I am tickled that it's wound up in the 'efficiency' category instead.
Remember when 'Use AI or lose your job' was the big thing, so everyone was tokenmaxxing, but as costs began to skyrocket (and revenues did not), companies started ditching flat subscription prices in favor of pay-per-token models? Turns out that gets real expensive, real fast , and suddenly it's become very important to, as the UK government put it, "consider if a simpler tool could do the job (for example, a spreadsheet or search engine)."
As far as practical impact, I think that being discourteous to AIs will be about as useful as worrying about how a late-night drive to the store will affect my personal carbon footprint while we're annihilating Gaza and building pipelines across the continent. But as another tacit acknowledgement that maybe our reliance on AI isn't quite all it's cracked up to be? I wholeheartedly endorse it.

title: Why so many Steam games have weirdly similar (and forgettable) names
text:
Duskfade. DUST: Origins. Dust Front RTS. Duskbloods. Dungeons of Dusk. These are all games that will be released in a 12-month period. I know the differences between them, but I'm convinced that no normal person would be able to remember all of these titles.
Dungeons of Dusk gets a pass, because it's a spin-off of a rad FPS that led the boomer shooter revival movement. That's easy enough to remember. Duskbloods is the new FromSoftware game, so there's no chance anyone will forget that.
But, I will pick on DUST: Origins and Duskfade . Want to know the origins of dust? That stuff gathering on your monitor and shelves? Dead skin (and other debris). That title stirs nothing within me, even though the game has some solid development pedigree behind it.
Duskfade is a perfectly pleasant 3D platformer with Kingdom Hearts-style combat that came out a couple of months ago. Once I've finished typing this paragraph, however, it will once again erase itself from my memory, because there's nothing evocative about the name.
So many video game names are either daft, interchangeable, or confusing. I got thinking about this because of a great thread by Hannah Flynn, communications director at Failbetter and a games marketing consultant. She's previously worked for brands like Penguin Books and Tate in the UK.
"Put aside what you think a game name should sound like," the advice reads. "There are thousands upon thousands of games on Steam now. Not all of them are named well, and there are weird trends which actually make your name less effective. Start with your game !"
That is surely the number one problem with most game names: people look at other games' names and try to pick something that sounds a bit like them. The result is often a flavourless mush that struggles to stay in the memory. To an outsider not already well-versed in the games marketplace, these often sound ridiculous.
The dust/dusk-relevant nugget I particularly like in Flynn's thread said to watch out for "filler" words like:
- "fall of" (11,527 results on Steam)
- "echoes of" (2,750 results on Steam)
- "shadow of" (8,243 results on Steam)
No offence to the developers of DUST: Origins, but 'origins' is absolutely of those words.
"There isn't a universal formula [for a good game name]," Flynn summarises. "But I like to think that a good name reflects the spirit of the game, and doesn't go out of its way to be un-memorable." She offers plenty of examples: Hades, Clickolding, Dave the Diver, Failbetter's own Sunless Skies.
This all resonated with me because I've been writing about games for 19 years, and I've seen a lot of bad game names in that time. A former colleague of mine used to bring up the games Violence Fight and Faster than Speed as being classically terrible titles for games—but those names are actually funny, whereas I think bland or generic names are much more annoying and widespread. In the Xbox 360 era where everyone wanted their version of Call of Duty or Gears of War, these proliferated.
Name that game
Hades is a great name for a game, let's face it. (Image credit: Supergiant) I decided to ask Flynn a bit more about the hypotheses shared in her thread, hoping to dig into the unhinged thought process behind every game name that ends with 'unleashed' or 'chronicles'. "I've thought about this more than is reasonable," Flynn says.
"I've been making indie games at Failbetter Games for 12 years, and have also reviewed hundreds of Steam store pages for other teams. I've developed this interest in game naming out of a professional need, but also because I'm getting older and my memory is getting worse, and I'd like to be able to recall the names of games I want to play."
I empathise with Flynn's point on age. One test is whether you can still remember what a game is called 10 minutes after you saw it announced in one of Geoff Keighley's showcases. Sorry *checks notes* TARAE: The Unbound, but even though I watched that trailer just one month ago at Opening Night Live, my memory had flushed that one away before the livestream was even over. A bad game name can trip a developer at the starting line.
TARAE looks pretty neat – it just didn't strike me as a great name for a game. (Image credit: Krafton) When developers look to other games to name theirs, "The possibility space spirals in on itself, and suddenly everything's called Rise of the Bonelord: Origins of Dust," she says.
"It's a fragment of a broader insularity in the industry. You can tell when games are only inspired by other games. I'm a big believer in looking to history, art, science, performance, nature, comics and pretty much everything else as inspirations for both making games, and naming them."
The reason a decent name matters, of course, is that we've got more of the things to choose from than ever. It's another way to make your game visible in the morass.
"Steam is a very densely populated platform these days," Flynn says. "To catch people's interest you only really have the name of your game and the capsule art, and there's only so much they can do. It's really an artform to create both and make them work well together in a way that stands out."
I asked GameDiscoverCo founder Simon Carless about this topic, who offers a slightly different take. "I think it's important that developers pick a name that's not too long and convoluted, and won't be immediately confused with another game. (The Outer Wilds vs. The Outer Worlds being the most famous of those name clashes.)
"Beyond that—I actually think that naming isn't that important, since most people buy a game based on video footage, someone else playing it, or a recommendation. And we've seen in music and elsewhere that weird names are in no way a blocker to becoming successful." Carless cites Steely Dan and Bananarama as examples.
Form vs function
Big Walk: they called it what you do in the game. (Image credit: Panic) So what defines a good name? "A good name sells the game's vibe," Flynn says. "The feel of how it'll play. There are loads of ways to be successful at this. It could come from a well-known phrase, an idiom, a place name, an artefact, a character's name, or just a concept that reflects the game's theme." Flynn cites a workbook called Don't Call it That , which has helped shape how she thinks about this.
"Finding the right name should feel like a jigsaw piece slotting into place, not that you've completed a 50-step escape room. Big Walk is about having a big walk. If you can, let the game name itself."
This got me thinking about whether the titles of my favourite indie games from the past few years were able to capture their essence. A few certainly did. Ball x Pit? That's a perfect name for that game. Dispatch? The word by itself isn't that evocative, but that does describe the basic act of what you do in the game, and it's simple enough to be memorable. Mouthwashing? That's a cleverly subversive name because it asks the question 'why is it called that?', which the game does pay off.
I think Carless' band analogy is apt—a name can seem clever in retrospect because it has already become iconic. Balatro is a good example of that to me. If LocalThunk's game had 10 reviews on Steam and was completely ignored, I'd probably call that a bad name. Few normal people, after all, would know that Balatro means 'jester' or 'clown' in Latin.
Flynn, though, points out that Balatro is actually a good game name by a few different criteria. "Balatro is a great case study. It's another word for Joker, which gets the seal of approval because it's historical and specific to the game. It's an alt-joker name for an alt-joker game. On the other hand its definition is comparatively little-known, even now, so it does have a slight whiff of thesaurus-digging.
"But! It's a jolly word, fun to say, easy to spell. It also comes from an established tradition. Puzzle-y games can get away with single-word names because of related media like board games (Ludo, Cluedo, Catan, Boggle) and traditional puzzle formats (Sokoban, Sudoku, Rubix). The fact that Balatro is called Balatro places it confidently in that tradition, versus calling it something like Crazy Jokers: Number Go Up, which overexplains the point and ultimately undersells the game to the kind of person who'd be into Balatro."
Flynn points out, too, that the name is so catchy that 'Balatro-likes' is now a widely used term for a whole range of roguelikes. Crazy Jokers-likes doesn't quite have the same ring.
"I think the name of a game can be the difference between someone remembering your game and having it disappear into the ether," says game trailer expert Derek Lieu . "Even if you ignore the fact a very generic name is less likely to show up at the top of search results, a title which sticks is just one more thing that can help it stand out."
Lieu praises SUPERHOT and Unpacking as elegant and memorable titles.
"'A Little to the Left' I think is a brilliant title because it's charming, has nice alliteration, and communicates the game's concept," Lieu adds. "'Tiny Glade' is great because it includes both scope and setting. 'Tokyo Jungle' I love because it's two words which don't belong together and I can't help but be intrigued."
The colon police
(Image credit: Failbetter Games) Concise game names are key, then, but many developers have succumbed to the temptation of throwing in some fancy punctuation and a rubbish subtitle.
"Game names with colons are for series, editions, and DLC," reads Flynn's thread on titles. "Don't give people two names to remember." Confidence is key to avoiding this.
"I think for indie teams, they're afraid of choosing one name and sticking with it," Flynn says about the temptation to dabble with Game: Subtitle naming conventions. "Usually, either side of the colon could work as a name on its own, but uncertainty wins out and they end up diluting their impact. In the end all they're doing is asking players to remember two names instead of one."
It's worth pointing out, too, that few of Flynn's rules are absolute, and that extends to colons. "There are times when you can use a colon without displeasing me, the colon police." A sequel with a returning main character, DLC, ultimate editions—Flynn says those all make sense.
Sometimes a subtitle can also be descriptive, which is useful to the player on a platform like Steam. "I love the name Iron Nest: Heavy Turret Simulator. The subtitle is in the game's name on Steam, so it clarifies what you're doing, but the key art just has this really impactful Iron Nest naming."
Failbetter's next game is called Mandrake —the result of lots of collaborative longlisting, Flynn says. As well as encapsulating horticultural and sorcerer-type themes, it's the name of the game's main character.
Carless says that there are some cases where a descriptive but unflashy game name only does the developer a favour in finding the right audience. "There are a small amount of cases when you can actually use SEO in the name of your game, e.g. if it's a farming game and you can stick 'farming' in there. But in general that's not possible. And... I don't think generic names are always bad if they have the right connotations. For example, if you make a job simulator game, I'm a fan of putting the word 'Simulator' in there. It anchors it…"
There's no precise formula to a great name, then, just an extensive series of best practices to avoid common mistakes. To turn Carless' band analogy on its head: you know a bad name when you're looking at it (Hoobastank). Tapping into the essence of what your game is, and not getting too preoccupied with what other developers are doing, seems like a sensible starting point.
"I hope that when people name their games, they do at least block out 5-10 possibilities and have a serious discussion about it," Carless says. "The first name you think of shouldn't always be the game name."

title: The algorithm comes for Steam's Discounts and Events
text:
More changes are coming to the way you buy games on Steam.
WHAT IT MEANS
Steam's Discounts and Events page is, as the name suggests, basically a collection of discounted games and special events: The Nier Franchise Sale, Game Devs of Color Expo, some lifts from your wishlist, and some that just match up with stuff you've done in the past. But all of them are "curated placements," which means they're scheduled by either developers or publishers themselves, or by Steam.
(Image credit: Valve) But Steam, as we all know, is always looking to refine the online game shopping experience, which is where these "dynamic and personalized" recommendations come in: "More discounted games or sale events will have the chance to be visible on the homepage and elsewhere on Steam, rather than be limited by a small, fixed number of slots."
Valve continues: "We have confidence this approach is better aligned with our goal, and results in a better experience for customers and developers. The constraint of a manually managed calendar doesn't make as much sense with such diverse customer tastes and so many relevant deals for customers available at any given time."
There was a bit of early confusion about what exactly Valve is doing here, and concerns that Valve would be pursuing the practice of dynamic pricing—that is, adjusting prices on the fly to reflect the demands of the moment. But it's the recommendations that are going dynamic, not the prices, so—assuming there are no unpleasant surprises in store—it's what you'll see that will be changing, not what you'll pay.
SEEMS FINE THEN?
At this early stage, yeah. Look, I'm a little tired of dancing to the tune of algorithms, and I wonder too if some people won't wind up missing out on cool stuff that maybe falls outside their usual areas of interest if they're only presented with what Steam knows they're likely to buy.
On the whole, though—and acknowledging that we don't have any details on how it will actually work just yet—it seems fine to me. Finding visibility on Steam is a never-ending challenge for indie developers, and if this puts more games in front of more eyeballs, it's hard not to see it as at least a small win.
None of this will be happening for a while, to be clear: A hard rollout date hasn't been set but Valve expects to start the process in early 2027.

title: Wardogs boss talks balance, XP, and why 'the endgame is sh*t' right now
text:
Dev Reacts: @jbowendaman made an awesome video that I thought warranted a response this morning about balancing and XP. Appreciate you all still playing our game, this video ended up longer than I thought! Link to orginal video: https://t.co/1tF0F9Mo94 pic.twitter.com/ERi8CltXVK September 29, 2026
A few notable quotes from Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer's latest Wardogs discussion video on X, in which he reacts to a video from YouTuber JbowenDaMan .
Wardogs continues to be one of my favorite games of the year, but almost three weeks into early access, I understand why developer Bulkhead was anticipating agita as players got deeper into its progression. The 100-player FPS has a serious XP grind , and some say they were having a better time before the most dedicated players started unlocking the highest tiers of vehicles, armor, and weapons.
Brammer's insights on player feedback and the studio's philosophy on balance are a useful lens into how Bulkhead sees its game—first and foremost a sandbox shooter where no two matches are the same, and not a competitive FPS that requires perfect balance.
"Sometimes in our game, we're going to be OK with something being a bit overpowered for a season and then underpowered next season, to keep it interesting," he said. "That doesn't mean I think level four armor is working, or that our balancing is great. I think the endgame is a bit sh*t."
(Image credit: Team17) It can be quite discouraging to face heavily-armored players with a pea shooter, or get smacked around by the strongest vehicles, so I'm curious what Bulkhead is considering to improve the endgame. Many think the thicker armors should go away entirely, and I admit I've had the same reaction when my killers shrug off six bullets to the chest, but that would rid the game of valuable build variety.
Wardogs firefights are asymmetrical by nature, and I wouldn't want to change that. While I'm unlocking stuff slower than the best players, the truth is that I'm also playing like a cheapskate—buying level two armor and cheaper guns because I don't want to risk a $20k loadout. Going into fights at a disadvantage is its own thrill, because I can still eat a bigger fish by getting the drop on them, and then become the bigger fish by looting their stuff.
Top of my mind is the changing playstyles of Wardogs week-to-week. Recently I've had a lot of matches where very few teammates want to do my favorite thing—push the Hot Zone and fight—and instead choose to focus on building or attacking FOBs. It can be frustrating to the point of not wanting to play, but as Jbowen and Brammer note, Wardogs is more fun when you're willing to adapt what you're doing to the current shape of the match. Instead of getting annoyed, I could try to pivot to hunting FOBs, learning anti-air, or practicing my pilot skills.
Brammer also reminded folks that Wardogs' planned metagame features will affect progression in the future. Bulkhead plans to add Tarkov-style skills that are improved through repetition, like tactical sprint duration and staying in-scope when cycling a sniper rifle bolt. Skills will be persistent, not wiped from season to season. In addition to cash and XP, a future "intel" resource will be used for unlocking gun parts and attachments that go beyond the current crop of grips, scopes, and muzzles.
"You're playing 25% of the game," as Brammer put it.
Sounds intriguing and intimidating. I really like how approachable Wardogs is right now, and my experience with full gunsmith systems in Battlefield 6 and CoD have me worried players will optimize guns until they're boring, but maybe Bulkhead's approach will be different.

title: The weird experience of liking a game before it's 'fixed'
text:
I was one of the weirdos who gave Battlefield 2042 a positive review at the same time as it was being called the worst Battlefield of all time.
Its detractors weren't wrong, we were just coming at it from different perspectives. BF 2042's giant 128-player maps did have desolate stretches where you could wind up stranded, hoofing it without cover, but I liked that. It created eerie, lonely moments that brought me back to playing Battlefield 1942, as did the glitchy hovercrafts (Battlefield games are supposed to have wonky physics!) and the goofy custom game modes you could make with the Portal scripting tool.
I could go on, but suffice it to say that I wasn't singing in the same key as the rest of the chorus, and EA launched an extended 'we're listening to your feedback' campaign, overhauling the maps and refocusing on 64-player modes to 'fix' the game. They weren't wrong to do it, but I didn't go back much.
I had a similar experience with No Man's Sky: What an odd game that was at launch, when it was engulfed in an inferno of criticism and accusations. Expectations for the endless space exploration game had gotten out of hand—thanks in part to some fuzzy marketing verbiage from developer Hello Games—but I remember liking the eerie solitude. (Maybe a pattern in my tastes is emerging here.)
No Man's Sky is now one of gaming's great redemption stories. Hello Games weathered that cosmic-scale scorn and remade it into a game that, for many, is much more like the game they'd wanted and expected back in 2016, with 32-player multiplayer and base building.
It's a great story, and Hello Games has earned a lot of respect for it, which funnily has us all smiling and clapping for the upcoming Light No Fire , another game inspiring enormous, probably too-high expectations.
But that original, 2016 version of No Man's Sky still sticks in my mind as a singular experience. Hello Games founder Sean Murray also remains fond of it.
"I've gone back to the original, played the game without any updates," Murray told us recently . "And I've got a real soft spot for it, to be honest. It's a more esoteric experience. It's a little bit weirder, but it's got its charm."
The post-launch work on both of these games obviously improved them for a lot of people, and in the case of No Man's Sky has resulted in a decade of happy spacefaring (fans even paid for a billboard ad to show their appreciation).
But I do lightly object to the common use of the word 'fixed' in the context of these overhauls, as if realigning a game's design is equivalent to solving a driver issue.
Murray got himself in trouble playing coy about the multiplayer features No Man's Sky didn't have in 2016, but it was still a cool game back then, and nothing has been quite like it since—not even No Man's Sky.

title: Ace Combat 8 Steam reviewers are steaming mad about its pre-order bonus not being a standalone app
text:
Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is technically out on Thursday, but as is commonplace now folks who pre-order the $90 deluxe edition get to hop into the cockpit a few days early. Anyone who pre-orders the $70 standard edition, meanwhile, gets a pretty sweet bonus: Ace Combat Zero, a 2006 entry in the series that has never been on PC before now. But how Bandai Namco has packaged Zero is now threatening to drag the new game's Steam review average down into Mixed territory.
Of the nearly 1,000 negative reviews as of this writing, there's a spread of complaints—performance, multiplayer connectivity, weightier flight physics, lacking HOTAS support—but one of the most common refrains is that the Zero bonus has been something of a bait-and-switch. As summarized by reviewer Akion :
"Before I bought the game the description said this about the Belkan War DLC Half the reason I got the game was because that is my all time fav. The integrity of this should matter to you.
"'*ACE COMBAT ZERO: THE BELKAN WAR is a standalone application separate from the ACE COMBAT 8: WINGS OF THEVE full game.'
"And now it says this:
"*ACE COMBAT ZERO: THE BELKAN WAR (Steam Version) is available as a DLC executable launched separately from the base game."
So why does this matter?
As another reviewer points out, "You need to install 140gb of data to play a 3gb 20 years old game." That's not an exaggeration: Ace Combat 8 is currently using up 140.24 gigs on my SSD, with the Zero DLC making up only 3.2GB of that total.
There's also a clear strain of dissatisfaction with the fact that on consoles, Zero comes along with its own achievements/trophies list, which is absent for the Steam version. Since it's tied to AC8, Zero also lacks separate cloud saves, something that would be pretty nice for playing it on the Steam Deck, where it should run very well given its age.
The lack of parity with the console version clearly has quite a few players annoyed, but the principle of the thing seems to be the biggest sticking point. The store page said Zero would be a separate app, and then it wasn't.
Some folks have countered that Bandai Namco couldn't release Zero as its own package due to the licensing terms of the planes featured in the game, seemingly based on this livestream featuring the developers on September 28 saying the licenses only permit giving the game away for free. But clearly it's possible to package the game separately on consoles even without selling it, and I'm skeptical it's impossible to find some kind of workaround on Steam. Hitman 3 still has a listing page, for example, despite not being purchasable by itself—it's listed as downloadable content for Hitman World of Assassination.
"Notice: At the request of the publisher, HITMAN 3 Access Pass: HITMAN 1 Complete First Season is unlisted on the Steam store and will not appear in search," reads a warning message at the top of the store page.
This criticism will soon show up in a smaller portion of Ace Combat 8's reviews as players who didn't bother to pre-order begin to filter into the reaction pool, but for now the pre-order bonus isn't quite the clean publicity win it otherwise could've been.

title: Deadlock's gigantic new update gives its city a spooky new coat of paint and debuts 6 new heroes, including the one and only Rat King
text:
The cursed city where Deadlock's battles take place just got even spookier than it already was in the City Never Sleeps update . Valve's second major overhaul for the invite-only MOBA marks another major step in its pseudo-early access development, giving it a much stronger visual identity than it had before, six striking new heroes, and a massive list of tweaks to how it plays.
Deadlock's entire map has been redecorated into three distinct themes: a bright city center, a haunted university, and a shadowy stock exchange. All the buildings and creeps that inhabit each street have been redesigned to fit in. There are pickle jars with hands growing out of them lurking in the heart of the map, sentient stacks of books in the right lane, and slimy trashbag monsters in the left lane.
Squeezed between it all are four districts with their own identities, like a theater district infested with literal stage hands pulling the strings on steampunk-style automatons. Atop the Chinatown district is a bell tower where teams can fight over a fountain of souls to try to get a currency advantage in a tight match. Even the wooden crates that players smash for resources are now padlocked and bolted shut.
It's a whole new playground that will take some time for players to fully figure out. In the meantime, Valve has prepared six new heroes who will be released based on a player voting system, just like the previous set . My money's on the Rat King taking the lead because, well, he's the Rat King, a crowned rodent that began as a fan concept a year ago and quickly became a meme in the community.
Don't get me wrong, though, the others look great, too. Valve made a nurse who holds a needle like a gun, a Chess master who seems to float like Overwatch's Zenyatta, a skeleton who found a rocket launcher, a cozy old witch who I do not trust, and a young artist who wields a paintbrush. Two heroes will drop each week with the first making their debut on Friday.
(Image credit: Valve) Here's some other big changes I see on the update page:
Player health bars are bolder and more readable than before
There are now small indicators to help you see where nearby teammates are
The kill feed is considerably more clear when it comes to seeing who took out who
The entire shop interface is way more intuitive and includes filters for finding what you need fast
There are several new ways to ping locations and objects on the map
Characters have double the amount of voice lines as before and you can listen to them in a new menu
New tools let you create bots to practice on and there's a more comprehensive breakdown of combat details for the nerds out there
There are new accessibility options, like custom UI colors, subtitles, and options to automatically move, mantle, and shoot
All of this is only a fraction of the things Valve has added to the game, some of which it's intentionally keeping a secret so players can discover them on their own. Despite the size of the update, Valve hasn't removed the need for an invite to play Deadlock. One has to wonder how many of these it will take before the game is finally released to the public so everyone can get a taste of what Valve's been cooking up.

title: Garry Newman adds necks to his neckless characters because the lack of necks 'comes up consistently in our many many many negative reviews'
text:
NECK NEWS FLASH: WHAT IS GOING ON WITH NECKS?
s&box is the spiritual sequel to Garry's Mod from creator Garry Newman and Facepunch Studios
Characters in s&box didn't have necks
Now they have necks
If you liked that they didn't have necks, you can adjust their necks so they don't have necks again
If you didn't like that they didn't have necks, maybe now you'll like them?
Why this big change from no necks to necks? For more, let's hear it straight from Mr. Newman:
Garry Newman
(Image credit: Garry Newman on YouTube) Garry Newman (pictured above, with a neck) is the creator of Garry's mod and founder of s&box developer Facepunch Studios.
" I've updated the citizen . They now have a default non frowny face and they can have a neck ."
"We have sliders to alter other aspects of the body like their chest, waist, neck, and nose size. You can choose their eye colour too. So if you liked having no neck, you can bring that back with a slider."
"Let me be honest here. I love the citizen, I love how he looks, I love that he has no neck ."
"But the feedback we've consistently got is that people hate them. They hate everything about them."
"So we're going to fidget around and change things to see if we can change that."
"Of course, this isn't what 'fixes' s&box on its own, but it something that comes up consistently in our many many many negative reviews, so it's something that we are addressing along with all the other feedback we receive."
You can read the rest of the patch notes for yourself, and I will update this article with any new, late-breaking neck-related facts as I uncover them.

Create a family, decorate a house, manage relationships and goals, have necks
PUBG
Drop in, gear up, and fight to be the last one standing with a neck
Corsair Cove
They're not easy to see because the pirates are so tiny, but most of them have necks

title: One of my all-time favorite games just announced an expansion, yet all I feel is fear
text:
"Core Values is the first paid DLC for Satisfactory and a major expansion," developer Coffee Stain studios announced on Tuesday, with the trailer above revealing that the construction sim is taking building deep underground for the first time, introducing "new resources, flora, fauna and more."
Here's how this news finds me: I should be Matt Berry in Toast of London convincingly shouting "Yes!" But instead, I'm Matt Berry in Toast of London saying "Yes! Yes!! Yes!? Yes!?!? Yesssss??? Yesssssss?????" over and over again, somehow increasingly unsure how to prounce a single syllable or what the word, in fact, actually means.
Compared to some of the dizzying hour counts some of my friends and colleagues have in life-consuming games like WoW and Dota 2 and Final Fantasy 14, my ~400 hours in Satisfactory across a few years is relatively mundane. I love the game, as I expressed in our 2024 Best Sandbox award . A small part of me is excited by the idea of going back to it. My building partner in crime and I left a monolith unfinished in our last world, with grand ambitions to route trains from across the entire map into one enormous central tower that would be visible from miles away. I do kind of want to finish it one day.
But another, bigger part of me knows that dipping back into Satisfactory for even a day will reignite the hunger . It'll be all I think about, all I want to play as soon as I log off work. No new games, no movies, just endless ways to optimize my construction chain for five more encased steel beams per minute.
I can never have enough encased steel beams. You understand that, right?
Perhaps there's a small amount of lingering Covid trauma tied up in this seed of dread, because I spent a good chunk of my lockdown months playing Satisfactory nearly every single day. But I still enjoyed playing a bunch of it in 2025, too. It's just that rare game that puts my brain in a vice grip as soon as I start thinking about it. One minute I'm having fun laying down some train tracks, the next I'm literally dreaming about how much we have left to build before we're "done."
Perhaps that's what's so scary about the announcement of a Satisfactory expansion: the blunt acknowledgement that it—and I—may never be done. Not when we're six feet under, or 600.
Core Values is coming "later," though it has a Steam page right now.

title: Making our favorite FPS modes 1v1 to decide the greatest of them all
text:
FOV 90
(Image credit: Future) Welcome to FOV 90, an FPS column from staff writer Morgan Park. Every other week, I cover topics relevant to first-person shooter enjoyers, spanning everything from multiplayer and singleplayer to the old and the new.
Organized FPS scrimmage is a time-honored tradition of PC gaming. Countless battles have been waged, friendships forged, and "GGs" exchanged in the name of contested territories, stolen flags, and almost-exploded explosives. FPS is my favorite genre because it's a canvas that accommodates endless modes of fun—formats that can happily coexist under the same banner to serve the current mood or group.
But if you had to choose just one, which would be the greatest FPS mode of them all?
That's what we're here to decide. We're pitting the greats against each other in a single-elimination tournament, voted on by readers like you. Round 1 starts now. Go go go!
Important Context
As you probably noticed, there are more FPS modes in existence than the 16 I've included here. This is not an exhaustive exercise, but a curated battle of the most established, enduringly popular FPS formats of past and present.
Broadly speaking, this is a tournament for modes that have appeared in many games, and does not include mode variants (Kill Confirmed, for example, is a variant of Team Deathmatch)
The bracket uses generic mode names, but well-known aliases for modes are mentioned further down , where relevant ("Slayer" is Halo's "FFA", for example)
The Bracket
Here are the lineups for Round 1. (Image credit: BracketHQ , Future) Round 1 - Vote!
Read up on the matchups below and vote for your favorite. Round 1 voting closes on Saturday, October 3 at 11:59 PM PDT . The more votes we get, the more interesting the results, so tell your friends! Next week we'll be back to share the results and begin Round 2.
Team Deathmatch or FFA/Deathmatch?
(Image credit: Microsoft) AKA: Team Slayer (Halo) // Slayer (Halo)
Would you rather fight alone or with a team?
Battle Royale VS Extraction
(Image credit: EA, BattleState Games) AKA: BR // Extraction Shooters
Two modes so large and complex that they've spawned vibrant subgenres.
Conquest VS Domination
(Image credit: EA, Microsoft) AKA: Warfare (Hell Let Loose) // Territories (Halo), Domination Control Point (Team Fortress 2)
Large-scale point capture with vehicles and control point respawns popularized by Battlefield, or small-scale point capture with random respawns popularized by Unreal Tournament and Call of Duty?
Bomb Defusal VS Hostage
(Image credit: Riot, Valve) AKA: Bomb (Rainbow Six Siege), Plant/Defuse (Valorant)
The single-life elimination showdown. Bomb is historically the more competitive mode, but many have a soft spot for escorting NPCs out of buildings.
Gun Game VS Payload
(Image credit: Microsoft, Valve) AKA: Arms Race (Counter-Strike), Escalation (Valorant)
Selfishly race to kill with every gun in the game, or push a cart down a track with a coordinated team?
Infection VS Prop Hunt
(Image credit: Microsoft, Valve) AKA: They're pretty much always called Infection and Prop Hunt.
Two asymmetrical party mode greats, but only one is moving on.
VIP VS Capture The Flag
(Image credit: Valve, Microsoft) AKA: VIP Escort (Call of Duty)
Two legendary objective modes in which one person becomes the most important, yet vulnerable member of the team.
Attack & Defend VS King of the Hill
(Image credit: Microsoft) AKA: 2CP (Overwatch), Breakthrough (Battlefield) // Headquarters (Call of Duty)
I expect this one to get spicy. Take turns attacking and defending on a singular front, or fight over one moving control point?

title: Amazon's $25 self-propelling speakers gave me the giggles as they tried to walk off the edge of my desk, and that's almost worth the price of entry alone
text:
Budget Win or Recycle Bin?
(Image credit: Future) Andy Edser is a man with a mission. It's a mission he didn't sign up for, or even want, but I'm his boss so he has to do what I say. And I'm making him test a ton of different cheap tech I might find on Amazon, AliExpress, TikTok Shop, or down the back of my sofa. Out of nowhere it will appear on his doorstep with no warning, and he has no choice but to use whatever it is like his life depends on it. Because it does.
Welcome to another episode of Budget Win or Recycle Bin, in which my editor sends me ultra-affordable products to review in an attempt to find decent PC gaming gear that costs less than the rest. Or to get his kicks by forcing me to test cheap rubbish, one of the two. This month, it's the turn of the Amazon Basics Stereo 2.0 desktop speakers —or as I like to call them, "the little speakers that almost could."
For a mere $25, you too could be the proud owner of a pair of surprisingly loud little desktop speakers. This miniature conical set is capable of an impressive amount of volume, in combination with some remarkably hefty bass given the diminutive driver size.
So much so, the units like to go for a little wander. All on their very own, as evidenced by my timelapse footage below:
Look at them go! Even when placed on a flat surface, I've found these speakers love to go running off on a little adventure. Crank the volume, turn your back, and you'll soon find them attempting to escape. Which is downright endearing if you ask me. I don't usually score these mini reviews by category, but for entertainment value? 10 out of 10, no notes.
Joking aside, I have plenty of positive things to say about this miniature set. As mentioned, the mere 2.4 Watt RMS figure is deceiving when it comes to actual perceived power output, and you could reasonably use them in a medium-sized room.
You'll want some double-sided sticky tape to keep them in place, lest you find them escaping out of your window...
They're also fairly weighty, which speaks well for build quality, although it still doesn't stop them from running for the hills when you put on a low-end heavy track.
Each unit also has some subtle blue LED lighting emerging from the bottom. I say subtle. What I mean is dim. But hey, it's better than "eye-searingly bright," like most cheap RGB-lit gaming gear. The split cable (you need to plug in both the USB Type-A and the 3.5 mm jack for the full lighting effect) is a reasonable length, and there's even a little in-line dial for adjusting the volume separately from your PC settings.
Future Future Future Future The real problem, unfortunately, comes in the form of frequency reproduction. There's an old (and slightly unfair) joke about Bose audio gear, which goes: "No highs, no lows, must be Bose." Well, the Amazon Basics set has highs and lows covered pretty comprehensively. It's the midrange, however, where these little speakers really fall off a cliff.
Listen to anything with distorted guitars, and this issue becomes immediately obvious. The midrange reproduction is pretty terrible, with a hollow, recessed valley of disappointment living bang in the centre of your tunes. The treble is a bit shrill and clattering, too, although the clarity is decent enough for gaming. If you keep the volume reasonable, and don't expect too much detail.
(Image credit: Future) But combine the edgy top end with the barren wasteland of midrange, add a hefty whack of overblown bass, crank to taste, and what you end up with is a set of surprisingly powerful, but still pretty cheap-sounding speakers. And you'll want some double-sided sticky tape to keep them in place, lest you find them escaping out of your window.
In all honesty, this Amazon Basics set has more going for it than I expected. For a mere $25, I thought I'd be testing a pair of tin-pot units with all the audio quality of a 1950s telephone speaker. These little beasties are better than the price tag suggests, but I still wouldn't recommend you buy a pair.
A set of cheap Creative Pebble units will cost you roughly the same amount of cash, and the drivers are much better balanced, albeit with lesser bass. Still, I've not had a fit of giggles while reviewing something for a while—and for the entertainment value of watching these Amazon speakers vibrate their way across my desk alone, I think I've had my fun this month.
Nice try, Dave. But I might keep this set around just for the party trick. Now, if only I could find the little blighters. Anyone looked under the sofa?
What I got...
Amazon Basics Stereo 2.0
Impressive bass, but the missing midrange is a real issue. There are a surprising number of alternatives at this price.
What I'd recommend...
Creative Pebble 2.0
Creative's little speakers look cuter, cost the same amount, and won't go for a wander.

title: You're hyped for Deadlock's new heroes and map updates, I'm hyped because of the 800 extra pre-match conversations, we are not the same
text:
I kinda wish Deadlock wasn't a MOBA —not because I don't play MOBAs, you understand. I have a misspent youth of over 2,400 hours in Dota 2 and 340 of the suckers in Deadlock itself. I know ball. Rather, I think Deadlock's universe and characters are so damn charming that I'd love for more people to know about them, and the MOBA genre is kinda unassailable.
And while the recent major Deadlock update has me kicking my feet and squealing at the gorgeous new environments—and I am very excited for Baba—there's one thing that makes me even happier: The voice lines. Not only does the update bring a voice line viewer into the game, it also… well, let me just let the official site speak for itself :
"Pre-match conversations between new and existing heroes increased from over 700 to 1500." It's Christmas , baby. Here are some of my favourites I've found so far:
These samples—the Drifter discovering a Lovecraftian god, Mina and Pocket being the most divorced couple in NYC, Celeste bargaining for her life, and Rem being a freaky little freak—are just some of the excellent conversations I've been flipping through since the update was released. Honestly, I've been digging into them for more time than I've been playing actual matches.
And the new cast of five heroes is only bound to add more excellent dynamics to Deadlock's roster—I can't, for instance, wait to see how the prolifically sassy capital punishment survivor Seven and park bench witch Baba interact, or how the "Be Not Afraid" doctor Nurse Harrow might interact with The Doorman, who could be a lovecraftian kindred spirit, for all we know.
These are just the pre-match conversation voicelines—"over 10,000 non-ping voice lines" have been added, too. It's a tremendous amount of work added to Valve's excellent MOBA, and I can't wait to see the Cursed Apple's final form… whenever that may be.
